name: LTC6102HVHDD#PBF
title: Precision zero-drift high-side current sense amplifier
summary: The LTC6102, LTC6102-1 and LTC6102HV are auto-zeroed high-side current sense amplifiers. An external RIN converts the shunt voltage into an output current IOUT = VSENSE / RIN, and a resistor ROUT from OUT to V– sets the ground-referred output voltage, so gain is ROUT / RIN. Offset is 10 µV maximum with 50 nV/°C maximum drift, so very small shunts can be used. The LTC6102 runs from 4 V to 60 V, the LTC6102HV from 5 V to 100 V, and the LTC6102-1 adds an enable pin; all come in 8-lead MSOP and 3 mm × 3 mm DFN.

pins.name: -INS
pins.function: Inverting input of the sense amplifier. Tied to -INF; the loop holds it at the potential of +IN.

pins.name: -INF
pins.function: Force input. Carries the current through RIN, which equals VSENSE / RIN; connect it to -INS close to RIN. RIN runs from V+ to this pin.

pins.name: EN
pins.function: LTC6102-1: enable, referred to V-. High turns the part on; low or open turns it off.

pins.name: OUT
pins.function: Open-drain current output. Sources into an external resistor a current proportional to the sense voltage; it is the same current that flows into -INF.

pins.name: VREG
pins.function: Internal regulated supply. Needs 0.1 µF or more between VREG and V+; it is not meant to power anything outside the part.

pins.name: +IN

circuits.title: 10A Current Sense with 10mA Resolution and 100mW Maximum Dissipation
circuits.description: High-side sensing of up to 10 A in a 1 mΩ shunt on a 5 V to 105 V supply. RIN = 20 Ω and ROUT = 4.99 kΩ give VOUT = 249.5 × VSENSE, which feeds an LTC2433-1 ADC running from 5 V; the ADC's serial lines go to a microprocessor. At 10 A the shunt drops 10 mV and dissipates 100 mW.
notes: VOUT = (ROUT / RIN) × VSENSE = 249.5 × VSENSE.
With a suitable shunt, currents above 1000 A can be monitored.

circuits.title: Kelvin Input Connection Preserves Accuracy with Large Load Current and Large Output Current
circuits.description: The shunt is a four-terminal part: its force terminals carry the supply (V+) and load current, and separate sense terminals feed RIN– (to -INS and -INF, joined right at RIN–) and RIN+ (to +IN). The supply pin connects to the V+ force side. Keeping high-current copper out of the sense paths stops trace resistance from adding to VSENSE or to RIN.

parts.note: four-terminal shunt, pins 1 and 2 force, 3 and 4 sense

notes: The shunt is a Vishay VCS1625-series part with four Kelvin pads.

circuits.title: Shunt Diode Limits Maximum Input Voltage to Allow Better Low Input Resolution Without Overranging
circuits.description: A Schottky diode across the shunt clamps VSENSE to its forward drop. A smaller RIN can then be used for finer low-current resolution while large currents no longer overrange the output; readings of the clamped high currents lose accuracy.

circuits.title: Second Input R Minimizes Error Due to Input Bias Current
circuits.description: Same Kelvin hook-up as the basic circuit with a second resistor, RIN+ = RIN– – RSENSE, in series with +IN. Matching the source resistance seen by both amplifier inputs cancels most of the bias-current error, leaving only the offset current times ROUT.

circuits.title: V+ Powered Separately from Load Supply (VBAT)
circuits.description: The shunt sits in a battery line VBAT while the part runs from its own V+ supply. This works as long as the load end of the shunt stays between V+ – 2 V and V+, and VBAT differs from V+ by no more than the input sense range.

circuits.title: LTC6102 Supply Current Monitored with Load
circuits.description: V+ is taken from the load end of the shunt rather than the battery end, so the part's own supply current passes through RSENSE and is measured along with the load. Because the input range includes V+, -INS and -INF settle at +IN = V+ and the circuit works normally; VSENSE itself is not limited by the sense range, only VSENSE / RIN by the allowed output current.

circuits.title: Voltage Level-Shift Circuit
circuits.description: A floating voltage VIN, stacked on a common-mode voltage VCM, is translated to a ground-referred output: VOUT = VIN × ROUT / RIN. The part's V+ and +IN sit at VCM and RIN goes to the top of VIN. VIN may be large as long as VIN / RIN stays inside the output current limit (1 V with RIN = 1k, 10 V with RIN = 10k).
notes: VOUT = VIN × ROUT / RIN.

circuits.title: Schottky Prevents Damage During Supply Reversal
circuits.description: A Schottky diode D1 from V– to ground blocks reverse current if the battery is connected backwards. It costs its forward drop VD in supply headroom at low battery voltage.

circuits.title: Additional Resistor R3 Protects Output During Supply Reversal
circuits.description: The reverse-supply circuit with a 1 kΩ resistor R3 between OUT and the ADC input. If the ADC's input clamp would pull the output to a high voltage while the supply is reversed, R3 limits that current.

circuits.title: LTC6102-1 with Enable Pulled Up Through 2.7M
circuits.description: With no logic supply for EN, a 2.7 MΩ resistor from the load side of the shunt pulls the enable pin up; the pin's internal ESD structure clamps it. At 60 V the resistor passes under 20 µA, enough for the enable input's bias current. RIN+ = RIN– – RSENSE balances the input bias currents.

circuits.title: Bidirectional Current Sense Circuit with Separate Charge/Discharge Output
circuits.description: Two LTC6102s share one shunt between a battery and a charger/load node, wired in opposite directions. U1 (RIN C, ROUT C) gives VOUT C for charging current and U2 (RIN D, ROUT D) gives VOUT D for discharge current. Each part takes V+ and its RIN from one end of the shunt and its +IN, through a matching 100 Ω, from the other.
notes: For IDISCHARGE ≥ 0: VOUT D = (ROUT D / RIN D) × RSENSE × IDISCHARGE.
For ICHARGE ≥ 0: VOUT C = (ROUT C / RIN C) × RSENSE × ICHARGE.

circuits.title: LTC6102 Monitors Its Own Supply Current
circuits.description: V+ connects to the load end of the shunt, so the part's supply current ISUPPLY flows through RSENSE together with the load current; R1 = 100 Ω and R2 = 4.99 kΩ set a gain of 49.9.
notes: VOUT = 49.9 × RSENSE × (ILOAD + ISUPPLY).

circuits.title: 16-Bit Resolution Unidirectional Output into LTC2433 ADC
circuits.description: An LTC6102-1 on a 4 V to 60 V supply with RIN = 100 Ω and ROUT = 4.99 kΩ (VOUT = 49.9 × VSENSE) drives pin 4 of an LTC2433-1 ADC whose reference is its 5 V supply, giving 2.5 V full scale. A POWER ENABLE line switches the amplifier on and off.
notes: VOUT = (ROUT / RIN) × VSENSE = 49.9 × VSENSE.
ADC full scale = 2.5V.
LTC2433-1 pins: 1 VCC, 2 REF+, 3 REF–, 4 IN+, 5 IN–, 6 GND, 7 CS, 8 SDO, 9 SCK, 10 FO.

circuits.title: Intelligent High-Side Switch with Current Monitor
circuits.description: An LT1910 high-side driver switches an SUB85N06-5 N-channel MOSFET feeding a load from 14 V, and an LTC6102 monitors the load current in a 5 mΩ shunt RS between the supply and the MOSFET drain. The LT1910's SENSE pin connects to the drain end of RS; FAULT is pulled up to VLOGIC through 47 kΩ and TIMER has 1 µF to ground. With 100 Ω and 4.99 kΩ, VO = 49.9 × RS × IL, which is 2.5 V at 10 A.
notes: VO = 49.9 × RS × IL; for RS = 5mΩ, VO = 2.5V at IL = 10A (full scale).
LT1910 pins: 1 GND, 2 TIMER, 3 FAULT, 4 IN, 5 GATE, 6 SENSE, 8 V+.

circuits.title: Input Overvoltage Protection
circuits.description: +IN is fed from the load side of the shunt through a 1 kΩ 3 W resistor, and an 18 V zener DZ (CMZ5931B, 1.5 W) connects +IN to V+, cathode at V+. A second 1 kΩ resistor sits in series with -INS, while -INF connects straight to RIN–.

circuits.title: Simple 500V Current Monitor
circuits.description: Current in a shunt on a 500 V rail. The LTC6102 V+ is on the 500 V rail; a 51 V zener (BZX884-C51) runs from that rail to a node with a 2 MΩ resistor to ground, the gate of P-channel MOSFET M2 and the anode of a BAT46 Schottky. The Schottky cathode, the source of M2 and the gate of P-channel MOSFET M1 are on V–. M1 carries the output current from OUT down to ROUT at ground, where VOUT = 49.9 × VSENSE. M1 and M2 are FQD3P50. Lethal voltages are present.
notes: VOUT = (ROUT / RIN) × VSENSE = 49.9 × VSENSE.

circuits.title: Remote Current Sense with Simple Noise Filter
circuits.description: The output current travels down a long wire to ROUT and COUT placed at a remote ADC. COUT across ROUT forms a low-pass filter with corner fC = 1 / (2π × ROUT × COUT).
notes: fC = 1 / (2 × π × ROUT × COUT).

operation.text: The internal amplifier drives an output MOSFET so that -INS follows +IN. With RIN from the supply side of the shunt to -INS, the shunt voltage appears across RIN and a current VSENSE / RIN flows in it. The amplifier inputs draw almost nothing (60 pA typical into -INS at 25°C), so that current goes through -INF and the MOSFET out of OUT, and a resistor from OUT to V– turns it into a ground-referred voltage. The output is analog and can be used directly or filtered.

LTC6102: 4 V to 60 V supply, 70 V absolute maximum. LTC6102HV: 5 V to 100 V supply, 105 V absolute maximum. LTC6102-1: the LTC6102 with an enable pin on pin 3 and a disabled supply current of 1 µA maximum. All are in 8-lead MSOP and 3 mm × 3 mm DFN.

The largest shunt is set by the peak sense voltage allowed: for 100 mV at a 20 A peak, RSENSE is at most 5 mΩ. The smallest useful shunt is set by the offset: with 3 µV typical offset and a 1 mA minimum current, a 3 mΩ shunt gives a signal equal to the offset. In the 20 A example a 5 mΩ shunt has 100 mV at peak (2 W) and an offset error worth 0.6 mA; a 0.5 mΩ shunt cuts the peak to 10 mV and 200 mW for an error of 6 mA (0.03% of full scale). The 3 µV offset gives 100 dB of dynamic range at 300 mV maximum sense voltage and over 116 dB at 2 V. For a 100 A, 60 dB system the minimum sense voltage can drop below 10 µV, so the peak can be 10 mV, 1 W in a 100 µΩ shunt, where a typical 100 mV design would dissipate more than 10 W; a special shunt could allow peaks over 1000 A.

Use Kelvin sense connections to the shunt in all but the lowest-power designs. A 10 mm × 10 mm square of 1 oz copper is about 0.5 mΩ: 2 A through it makes a 1 mV error (1% of a 100 mV signal), 10 A makes 5%, and copper's resistance changes by more than 0.4%/°C. A shunt with built-in Kelvin terminals is best. The input is itself Kelvin: current flows into -INF while -INS carries only bias current, so -INS should run as its own trace to the point at RIN and the two pins should be joined as close to RIN as possible. The high end of RIN goes straight to the positive terminal of the shunt. Done this way RIN can be as low as 1 Ω; below 10 Ω a four-terminal RIN gives the best accuracy. Trace resistance adds to RIN and its copper tempco becomes a gain drift.

RIN sets the transconductance, IOUT = VSENSE / RIN; with RIN = 100 Ω, 100 mV gives 1 mA. Pick RIN so the largest expected sense voltage gives IOUT = 1 mA, the output available at low supply, for the widest output range; a larger RIN lowers output current and dissipation. A smaller RIN can be used to resolve small currents if large ones are limited some other way, for example a Schottky diode across the shunt, at the cost of accuracy at high current.

VOUT = IOUT × ROUT. Choose ROUT so that IOUT(MAX) × ROUT stays within the part's maximum output voltage and within the input range of whatever OUT drives. ROUT is also the output impedance: a high-impedance load can take nearly any value, but a low-impedance load or an ADC that draws current spikes may need a lower ROUT (a load of 100 × ROUT costs 1%).

Auto-zero circuitry clocked at about 10 kHz keeps the DC offset near zero over temperature, sense voltage and supply. The offset adds straight to VSENSE; at 3 µV typical it can usually be ignored, and its very low drift lets it be calibrated out for very wide dynamic range. Clock feedthrough takes two forms: settling of the internal sampling capacitor, input referred and independent of the resistor values, with a residue under 1 µVRMS at 10 kHz; and charge injection current spikes multiplied by the impedance at the inputs, reduced by smaller gain-setting resistors and low source resistance.
The averaged charge-injection spikes dominate the DC input bias current below 70°C. Above 70°C leakage of the input ESD diodes takes over, and both input bias currents grow and flow into the pins.

The output delivers at least 1 mA and can give more, all of it drawn through RIN into -INF, so at maximum supply and output current the dissipation can exceed 100 mW. Work out the worst-case dissipation, multiply by θJA and keep the die below 150°C. Example: MSOP at 55 V ±5 V with 1 mA out at 80°C: PQ(MAX) = 39 mW, POUT(MAX) = 60 mW, PTOTAL ≈ 99 mW, die at 100°C; at 125°C ambient the die reaches 145°C. Supply current rises with temperature. The DFN's lower θJA runs much cooler. The LTC6102HV at up to 105 V dissipates more for a given current, further limiting output current at high ambient temperature. Limit the output current with the shunt and RIN values, and add an external clamp where input faults are likely.

VOUT = IOUT × ZOUT, so any impedance on OUT shapes the response. A capacitor across ROUT makes a low-pass filter that reduces noise and also acts as a charge reservoir for a switching load such as a multiplexer or ADC.

The inputs work from V+ down to V+ – 2 V. The shunt can therefore be in a line other than the supply (VBAT), provided the gap between VBAT and V+ stays within the input sense voltage range of the electrical characteristics.

operation.topic: Voltages above V+ and level translation
operation.text: The part can measure voltages above its own supply as long as the negative end of the input is within the input sense range. With V+ on the load end of the shunt, -INS and -INF settle within a few microvolts of +IN = V+ and the part's supply current is measured too. VSENSE can then be large; only VSENSE / RIN must stay within the output current rating, and ROUT/RIN may give gain or attenuation. The input can be a voltage source: 1 V with RIN = 1k, or 10 V with RIN = 10k; RIN = 10k and ROUT = 5k let the LTC6102HV translate a 10 V input to 5 V at up to 100 V common mode. With a large RIN, a matching resistor in series with +IN reduces bias-current error.

There is no internal protection against a reversed supply. A Schottky diode in series with V– limits the reverse current, at the cost of its drop VD in supply headroom. If OUT drives something that would clamp it to a high voltage during reversal (an ESD clamp, for example), connect OUT through a resistor or Schottky diode.

With very little output current, an input step can produce a delay before the output starts to move; raising the minimum output current (a larger RSENSE or smaller RIN) shortens it. The step-response curves are labelled with the initial output currents. On a fast input the amplifier slews the output FET gate; a smaller RIN lets the output current rise faster and raises the maximum output current, and a larger ROUT also speeds the output voltage. Both raise the voltage gain.

The feedback resistance of the internal loop is the output MOSFET's 1/gm, which falls as -INF current rises and is on the order of 10 kΩ at 1 mA. The loop gain is 1/(RIN × gm), so bandwidth is about GBW × RIN × gm, up to about 2 MHz. Smaller RIN and smaller IOUT generally lower the bandwidth; choose VSENSE and RIN for the most IOUT and closed-loop gain. The theoretical maximum is VIN = 10 VDC with RIN = 10k (IOUT = 1 mA, gain near 1). gm follows the DC value of IOUT, so adding DC current to a small AC input raises the bandwidth.

VREG is an internal supply near V+ for internal bias, not for external circuits. Connect 0.1 µF between VREG and V+, placed very near the part. Where supply transients are large, a 6.8 V zener can be added across this capacitor.

EN is a logic input referred to V– that accepts TTL levels whatever V+ is. High turns the part on; low or open turns it off with very little supply current. When high it draws a few microamps. Without a logic supply it can be pulled to V+ through a large resistor; the built-in ESD structure clamps the pin like a zener. Keep that current to a few milliamps or less for long-term reliability, and lower to save power, but high enough for the enable bias current: 2.7 MΩ at 60 V gives less than 20 µA.

At power-up or enable, current goes to three things: charging the VREG capacitor (nominally 0.1 µF) to about 4.5 V below V+, which can take significant current; the amplifier's supply current, little higher than in normal operation; and the output, which may briefly go high and pass milliamps through RIN into ROUT and the output's ESD limiting structure until the loop settles. When the LTC6102-1 is disabled the amplifier is off and the VREG capacitor discharges very slowly, so short disable periods save start-up energy and the part restarts faster.
